description_full: Vulcan Materials Company produces and supplies construction aggregates in the United States. It operates through three segments: Aggregates, Asphalt, and Concrete. The company provides crushed stone, sand and gravel, sand, and other aggregates for use in construction and maintenance of highways, streets, and other public works, as well as in the construction of housing and commercial, industrial, and other nonresidential facilities; aggregates that are used as ballast for construction and maintenance of railroad tracks; riprap and jetty stones for use in erosion control along roads and waterways; asphalt mix; asphalt construction paving services; and ready-mixed concrete products. The company was formerly known as Virginia Holdco, Inc. and changed its name to Vulcan Materials Company. Vulcan Materials Company was founded in 1909 and is headquartered in Birmingham, Alabama.

financial_summary: Vulcan Materials Company (Holdi is a large-cap basic materials business with a $36.3B market cap on $7.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, with gross margins sitting at 25%.

The business throws off $1.1B in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.68× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.8×.

Shareholder yield is only 1.9%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 12% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 15% below the high.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $119 (margin of safety -138%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 25%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $89.49 to $159 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/E 33.5 vs 16.5, EV/EBITDA 18.2 vs 8.5 and P/FCF 32.0 vs 22.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 2% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $313 on average, 11% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 9% earns above the cost of capital of 8.4%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.61).
It runs a 25% gross margin and converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 9/9 and cash conversion of 1.68x.
ROE of 13% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.8% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.8x net debt to EBITDA ($183.3M of cash against $4.4B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.8x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.1, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.8% over 3 years, 10.3% over 5 years and 8.8% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 41% of profits supports about 3.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.9% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 8.5% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 24, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (12 sales, net $14.5M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.9% (1.2% in buybacks and 0.7% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 7.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 11,548 employees, each generates about $688K of revenue, in line with the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 7.0% a year.
That works out to $98K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.4M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
